Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
245 PM EDT Sat Jul 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 242 PM EDT Saturday...

Little to no changes with regards to a pattern shift towards more 
showers and thunderstorms next week.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 242 PM EDT Saturday...

1. Gradually increasing rain and storm chances for the new week.

2. Multiple rounds of rain mid-week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 242 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Mostly dry conditions are expected today into tonight. 
Modest radiational cooling will be offset by incoming high clouds, 
overnight. Mid 50s to mid 60s are expected early tomorrow morning, 
with perhaps a few cool hollows in the upper 40s. On Sunday, surface 
high pressure that has locked our region beneath a dry, stable air 
mass will shift farther out to sea. High temperatures will rise into 
the upper 70s to mid 80s for Sunday. Increasing moisture is 
expected, mainly over northern New York while a subtle trough angles 
south of the Adirondacks. 250-750 J/kg of CAPE will develop with 
daytime heating with weak flow aloft. Isolated to scattered showers 
and thunderstorm will be possible across northern New York, while 
Vermont will remain mostly dry. Showers will likely favor terrain 
boundaries, drift off their point of initiation, and generally 
decay. With slow-movers, a few brief downpours could occur. With the 
loss of daylight, shower activity will decrease, though perhaps not 
entirely 0 percent. Mid 50s to mid 60s are expected still.

Monday will be a rinse-and-repeat, but everything will have shifted 
slightly east. With increasing surface dewpoints, we could eke out 
closer to 500-1000 J/kg of CAPE, but there will be little shear 
present. Northern New York will remain the primary focus for 
convection, with fewer cells across Vermont. Some surface confluence 
will be present, but there won't be any upper feature. Convection 
will remain garden variety with somewhat higher potential for 
localized downpours due to the greater extent of rain and slowly 
increasing PWATs.

Then Tuesday will also be largely the same. A stronger upper level 
vort will approach from the west, but its influence won't creep into 
the area until relatively late on Tuesday or even Tuesday 
night/Wednesday. Forecast scenarios diverge, with the main 
differences being the strength and intensity of the incoming surface 
low. Most guidance favors a deep, sub 1000mb surface low closing off 
near Lake Ontario with the occlusion process resulting in briefly 
erratic motions before it shuffles east. A minority favors a weaker 
system with a surface low not developing until the upper trough is 
moving offshore. All told, there will be chances for showers and 
thunderstorms with little change to shear or instability regardless 
of which forecast scenario you pick. Localized downpours will be 
possible, mainly wherever surface convergence aligns with increasing 
upper divergence in association with the developing upper low.

KEY MESSAGE 2: An upper level low builds into the region for middle and 
late week and brings periods of rain. It looks to move slowly from 
west to east Tuesday through Thursday, and the time of its exit is 
still very uncertain. A relatively potent surface low should form 
along it and bring an area of consistent rainfall, but its exact 
position is uncertain. The solution favored by most EPS members puts 
the bullseye over central/southern Vermont, where probabilities of 
2, 3 and 4 inches of rain are 50-70, 20-50 and 10-20 percent 
respectively. This could lead to a flood threat that would need
to be watched carefully. A saving grace is that the precipitation
won't be as convective after Monday, something that would cut 
down on rainfall rates. PWATs look to be in the 1.3-1.5 inch 
range, sufficient for heavy rain but not overly high as the 
trough is northern stream. The GEFS/CMCE ensembles favor the 
track of the surface low over coastal New England and keep the 
probability of 3 inches under 10 percent, and the probability of
2 inches in the 10-40 percent range, something less concerning 
given the relatively long time of the precip and lower rates. 
The rain should become more scattered and diurnally driven late 
week and into the weekend, but isolated to scattered afternoon 
showers will still be possible.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 18Z Sunday...VFR conditions are expected to mostly prevail
for the next 24 hours. The one exception will be at MPV and SLK
where fog formation is possible late in the night. The probability
of a period of MVFR visibility is around 60-70 percent, and the
probability of a period of IFR visibility is maybe around 40-50
percent. The fog lifts by 12Z. Winds will be southerly at BTV and
PBG today and tomorrow, and generally light and variable elsewhere.
All terminals will go light or terrain driven tonight.

Outlook...

Sunday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Monday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Monday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Tuesday: VFR. Definite SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Likely SHRA,
Chance TSRA.
Wednesday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Likely SHRA, Chance
TSRA.
Wednesday Night: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: Mainly IFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
